sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \mathcal{C}] to [MATH: \mathcal{B}] is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \mathcal{B}] to [MATH: \mathcal{C}.] Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of [MATH: P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}},] we get

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given two bases [MATH: \color{blue}\mathcal{B}] and [MATH: \color{red}\mathcal{C}] of a vector space [MATH: V,] the change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \color{blue}\mathcal{B}] to [MATH: \color{red}\mathcal{C}] is the matrix [MATH: P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},] whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from [MATH: \color{blue}\mathcal{B}] relative to the basis [MATH: \color{red}\mathcal{C}].

Content:
In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
[MATH: |||||; [b_{1}]_{C}|[b_{2}]_{C}|…|[b_{n}]_{C};|||||]

Content:
For example, let's consider two bases [MATH: \mathcal B] and [MATH: \mathcal C] of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.]

Content:
If we happen to know that

Content:
[MATH: [− 12; 11]]

Content:
then the change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \mathcal{B}] to [MATH: \mathcal{C}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: P_{B → C} =|[− 12|3; 11|6].; ↑_([b_{1}]_{C})↑_([b_{2}]_{C})]

Content:
The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector [MATH: [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}] in the basis [MATH: \mathcal C] via the transformation

Content:
[MATH: [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.]

Content:
This can be visualized as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dd5edf0aea2275637a6fcc193284cb56]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The coordinates of the vectors in [MATH: \mathcal{C}] relative to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}] are
[MATH: [− 4; 1]]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \mathcal{C}] to [MATH: \mathcal{B}] is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of [MATH: \mathcal{C}] relative to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}.]

Therefore, we obtain
[MATH: [− 4|5; 1|7]]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Inverse of a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

Content:
Since the columns of a change-of-coordinates matrix are linearly independent, the matrix must be invertible.

Content:
In fact, the change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \color{blue}\mathcal{B}] to [MATH: \color{red}\mathcal{C}] and the change-of-coordinates matrix from [MATH: \color{red}\mathcal{C}] to [MATH: \color{blue}\mathcal{B}] are the inverses of each other:

Content:
[MATH: P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.]

---
